caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: North Macedonia's debt has risen steadily: 30.6% of GDP in 2006 (20.6% in 2008, the low), 50.8% in 2020 after COVID, 50.4% in 2022, and a projected series high of 52.5% in 2025 (52.9% in 2024). The drift reflects persistent deficits and slower growth rather than crisis borrowing. GDP grew from $6.9bn in 2006 to a projected $19.1bn in 2025. The denar's peg to the euro anchors policy; debt at just over 50% of GDP is manageable but the upward trend bears watching given the narrow export base.
inflation_management: The denar's peg to the euro makes North Macedonia an importer of euro-area monetary conditions. Inflation was -0.8% in 2009 (the low), 1.2% in 2020, then 14.2% in 2022, the series high, on food and energy imports — well above the euro-area average. It fell to 3.5% in 2024 and is projected at 4.1% for 2025, slower disinflation than the area as food prices and wages stayed firm. The central bank shadows ECB moves to defend the peg; domestic adjustment runs through fiscal policy.

key_events.event: Global financial crisis; the euro peg held through the regional downturn.
Political crisis (2015-17) resolved by the Prespa Agreement (2018), unblocking NATO and EU paths.
Joined NATO (March 2020); COVID-19 pushed debt to 50.8% of GDP.
Inflation hit 14.2%, the series high, on imported food and energy prices.
EU accession talks opened (2022) but stalled over bilateral disputes; debt projected at 52.5% of GDP.

outlook_next_decade: North Macedonia's outlook is the EU-accession story: unblocking talks would anchor reform and investment, while the current stall is the main drag. The euro peg provides stability but no monetary flexibility. Debt just above 50% of GDP is sustainable if deficits narrow; the structural risks are emigration, a narrow industrial base, and energy dependence. Inflation should track toward euro-area levels as food-price pressures ease.
